title: What Is a Trust Framework, and How Does It Decide Who Can Issue and Verify Digital Credentials?
summary: The future of interoperable digital identity depends on more than shared formats and protocols, it depends on the governance layer that defines trust, accountability, and assurance.
body_markdown:
Imagine a Utah verifier presented with a mobile driver’s license issued by California. Matching data formats and a shared presentation protocol get the two systems talking. They do not answer the question the verifier actually cares about: should I trust what this credential says, and who is accountable if it turns out to be wrong? Answering that is the job of a trust framework. It is the governance backbone that turns technical interoperability into something a relying party can act on.


## What a trust framework contains


A trust framework is a written agreement about who is trusted to do what, and under which conditions. It typically specifies six things: the roles participants can hold (issuer, holder, verifier, and often a governing authority), the assurance levels those roles must meet, the certification process that admits a participant, ongoing audit, allocation of liability when something goes wrong, and dispute resolution.


[NIST Special Publication 800-63-3](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , the U.S. Digital Identity Guidelines, gives the assurance vocabulary most frameworks reuse. It separates identity proofing (Identity Assurance Level, or IAL), authentication (Authenticator Assurance Level, or AAL), and federation (Federation Assurance Level, or FAL), so that a framework can require, for example, in-person proofing at IAL3 for one use case and self-asserted attributes at IAL1 for another. The[Kantara Initiative](https://kantarainitiative.org/us-identity-certification-program/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) shows the certification half: it runs an assurance program that approves identity service providers through accredited assessors and issues classes of approval that a relying party can verify. Definitions describe what “good” looks like; a framework decides who has demonstrated they meet it.


## A trust framework is not a trust list


A trust framework and a trust list are related but distinct, and conflating them is a common source of confusion in digital ID governance. The framework is the governance: rules, obligations, and accountability. The trust list is the machine-readable output of those rules: the signed roster of keys or providers that a verifier’s software checks at the moment of verification.


The eIDAS regulation makes the difference concrete. Article 22 obliges each EU member state to publish a trusted list of its qualified trust service providers, sealed and formatted for automated processing. That list has, in the regulation’s language, a “constitutive effect”: a provider is qualified only if it appears on it. But the list is downstream of the framework. A provider lands on it only after a national supervisory body oversees it, and an accredited auditor performs a conformity assessment. The list tells a verifier which keys to accept, the framework explains why those keys earned their place, and the mechanism can remove them if an issuer fails an audit. A trust list without a framework behind it is just a file.


## eIDAS shows what a legislated framework looks like


The European Digital Identity Regulation,[Regulation (EU) 2024/1183](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1183/oj/eng?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , is a mature example of a trust framework written into law. Published in the Official Journal on April 30, 2024, and in force since May 20, 2024, it requires every member state to offer at least one European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet to citizens and residents by the end of 2026. It does not stop at mandating a wallet. Implementing regulations adopted since late 2024 specify wallet functionality, rules for issuing and revoking personal identification data and electronic attestations of attributes, protocols for cross-border interoperability, and certification requirements that wallets must satisfy. In other words, the regulation defines the roles, assurance obligations, credential-issuer certification path, and accountability structure, and then lets the trusted lists and technical profiles follow.


## Why frameworks are the policy lever


For a policy lead or agency PM, the trust framework is the lever you actually control. Formats and protocols are usually inherited from open standards; the framework is where a jurisdiction sets its own terms. Two mechanisms carry most of the weight.


The first is certification.[Certified wallets](https://blog.spruceid.com/digital-wallet-certification-the-foundation-for-interoperable-state-identity-systems/) and credential issuer certification are how a framework enforces its rules before anything reaches a resident. A wallet that passes certification has demonstrated the security and privacy properties the framework demands; an issuer that passes has demonstrated its proofing and key-management practices. The second is procurement. When an agency writes framework conformance and certification into a solicitation, it converts governance into a contractual obligation a vendor must meet to win the work. That is how open standards and accountability move from principle into deployed systems, and it is why[interoperability is a policy decision, not only a technical one](https://blog.spruceid.com/interoperability-is-a-policy-decision-not-just-a-technical-one/) .


## What a trust framework does not do


A trust framework is necessary but not sufficient on its own. It does not specify cryptographic formats or transport protocols; those are defined by standards such as[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , the[W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , and OpenID for Verifiable Presentations. It does not guarantee that two frameworks in different jurisdictions recognize each other; cross-border reliance still requires an explicit mapping or a mutual recognition agreement. And it does not remove human judgment from edge cases, which is why dispute resolution is one of its named components. The framework decides whose[verifiable digital credentials](https://blog.spruceid.com/digitalidentity-how-do-verifiable-digital-credentials-work-a-non-technical-explanation/) count. Making them technically legible is a separate job, done well only when both are in place.
